explanation: Medicines for digestion and body chemistry: diabetes, obesity, reflux, nausea, bowel and liver problems, vitamins and minerals.
Reduce, neutralize or shield against stomach acid, relieving heartburn, acid reflux and stomach ulcers.
Treat stomach ulcers and reflux (acid rising into the food pipe), mainly by reducing stomach acid or protecting the lining.
Block the pumps in the stomach lining that release acid, relieving heartburn and reflux.
Ease gut problems without visible damage, such as cramps, bloating or slow stomach emptying.
Ease cramps, spasms, bloating and other gut problems without visible damage, for example by relaxing gut muscle.
Block acetylcholine, a nerve signal driving gut muscle and glands, relaxing spasms or reducing secretions while barely entering the brain.
Prevent or relieve nausea and vomiting, for example from cancer treatment, surgery or motion sickness.
Prevent or relieve nausea and vomiting, for example from cancer treatment, surgery or motion sickness.
Block serotonin, a messenger from the gut that triggers vomiting, to prevent nausea and vomiting from chemotherapy.
Anti-nausea medicines that are not serotonin (5HT3) blockers, preventing or relieving nausea and vomiting by other means.
Treat diseases of the liver and of bile, the digestive fluid the liver makes and the gallbladder stores.
Treat problems of bile, the liver's digestive fluid, for example by supplying bile acids, increasing bile flow or dissolving gallstones.
Supply bile acids, the fat-digesting part of bile, or modified versions of them, for liver, bile or bile acid disorders.
Bile medicines that fit none of the named bile therapy groups, used for problems of bile, the liver's digestive fluid.
Treat liver disease by protecting or supporting the liver, or by helping it process fat (lipotropics).
Protect or support the liver, aiming to limit damage or improve its function in liver disease.
Relieve constipation (hard or infrequent stools), for example by softening stools, drawing water into the bowel or speeding gut movement.
Relieve constipation (hard or infrequent stools), for example by softening stools, drawing water into the bowel or speeding gut movement.
Block opioid painkillers' effect on the gut but not the brain, easing their constipation without undoing pain relief.
Constipation medicines that fit none of the named groups, relieving hard or infrequent stools in other ways.
Act mainly within the gut to treat diarrhea, calm bowel inflammation or clear gut infections.
Kill germs inside the gut while barely entering the blood, for example treating bowel infections.
Kill bacteria or fungi within the gut while barely entering the blood, for example treating bowel infections.
Slow the movement of the bowel to ease diarrhea, typically acting on its opioid receptors, the targets of opioid painkillers.
Slow the movement of the bowel to ease diarrhea, typically acting on its opioid receptors, the targets of opioid painkillers.
Calm inflammation of the digestive tract, mostly acting locally, for example in inflammatory bowel disease.
Steroids that calm inflammation or immune activity mainly within the digestive tract, with less effect elsewhere in the body.
Help people with obesity lose weight, acting on the brain's appetite control or elsewhere in the body.
Help people with obesity lose weight, acting on the brain's appetite control or elsewhere in the body.
Act on the brain's appetite control to reduce hunger and food intake, helping weight loss in obesity.
Aid weight loss in obesity by acting in the body rather than on the brain's appetite control.
Medicines for obesity that fit none of the named groups, used to help people lose weight.
Help digest food when the body makes too few digestive enzymes or too little stomach acid.
Help digest food when the body makes too few digestive enzymes or too little stomach acid.
Supply digestive enzymes, such as those breaking down fat, protein or starch, when the body makes too few.
Mostly lower blood sugar in diabetes; some are also used for heart failure, chronic kidney disease or obesity.
Replace or add to the body's own insulin, the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into cells.
Start working quickly and last a few hours, covering the rise in blood sugar after meals.
Act more slowly and longer than fast-acting insulin, up to about a day, giving background blood sugar control.
Contain a quick and a slower insulin, so one injection covers a meal and gives longer background control.
Work steadily for about a day or longer, giving background blood sugar control.
Supply insulin through the lungs, breathed in rather than injected, to control blood sugar.
Non-insulin medicines lowering blood sugar, mainly in type 2 diabetes; some also treat obesity, heart failure or kidney disease.
Make the pancreas release more insulin, lowering blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.
Combine two or more blood sugar-lowering medicines taken by mouth in one product, for type 2 diabetes.
Make the body's cells respond better to insulin (reduce insulin resistance), lowering blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.
Block an enzyme that breaks down gut hormones which boost insulin after meals, lowering blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.
Mimic a gut hormone that boosts insulin and curbs appetite, lowering blood sugar in type 2 diabetes; some treat obesity.
Make the kidneys pass extra sugar into urine, lowering blood sugar in diabetes; some treat heart failure or kidney disease.
Blood sugar-lowering medicines other than insulin that fit none of the named groups, used mainly in type 2 diabetes.
Diabetes medicines that are neither insulins nor blood sugar-lowering drugs, treating diabetes or its complications in other ways.
Diabetes medicines that fit none of the named groups, treating diabetes or its complications in other ways.
Supply vitamins, nutrients the body needs in small amounts but cannot make enough of, mainly preventing or treating shortages.
Single-vitamin products fitting none of the named vitamin groups (A, D, B1, C), mainly for preventing or treating vitamin shortages.
Single-vitamin products fitting none of the named vitamin groups (A, D, B1, C), mainly for preventing or treating vitamin shortages.
Supply essential minerals, mainly to prevent or correct a shortage in the body.
Supply potassium, a mineral vital for nerves, muscles and the heart, for example when blood levels are low.
Supply potassium, a mineral vital for nerves, muscles and the heart, for example when blood levels are low.
Medicines for digestion or metabolism (body chemistry) fitting none of the other named digestive and metabolic groups.
Medicines for digestion or metabolism (body chemistry) fitting none of the other named digestive and metabolic groups.
Medicines that are amino acids, protein's building blocks, or compounds derived from them, mainly for problems of body chemistry.
Supply an enzyme, or help the body make one, making up for a faulty enzyme, mainly in inherited metabolic diseases.
Other medicines for digestion or metabolism (body chemistry): those that are neither amino acids nor enzymes.
Medicines that prevent clots, stop bleeding (as in hemophilia), treat anemia or other blood disorders, or supply fluids and nutrition.
Prevent or dissolve blood clots, lowering the risk of heart attack, stroke and clots in the veins or lungs.
Prevent or dissolve blood clots, lowering the risk of heart attack, stroke and clots in the veins or lungs.
Prevent and treat blood clots with heparin or related agents, which act mainly through the blood's own clot-blocking protein.
Stop platelets (tiny clotting cells) clumping, preventing heart attacks and strokes; some treat high blood pressure in the lungs.
Use enzymes to dissolve blood clots, as in heart attack or stroke, or to curb clotting in other ways.
Directly block thrombin, the enzyme that forms clots, to prevent or treat blood clots.
Directly block factor Xa, a key clotting protein, to prevent or treat blood clots.
Medicines against blood clots that fit none of the named groups, preventing or treating clots in other ways.
Stop or prevent bleeding, for example in hemophilia, during surgery or when platelet counts are low.
Block protein-cutting enzymes that break down blood clots or tissue, helping stop bleeding or limit tissue damage.
Block proteinases (protein-cutting enzymes), for example those dissolving clots, to curb bleeding or tissue damage.
Help blood clot to stop bleeding, for example by replacing missing clotting factors, boosting platelets or sealing surgical wounds.
Applied directly to a bleeding surface, for example during surgery, to help form a clot or seal.
Replace missing clotting proteins, or add a gene to make them, in hemophilia and other bleeding disorders.
Anti-bleeding medicines acting through the bloodstream, not applied locally, that fit none of the named groups.
Treat anemia (too few healthy red blood cells), supplying what the body needs to make them or boosting their production.
Replace iron, which the body needs to make red blood cells, to treat anemia caused by iron deficiency.
Replace iron by mouth with ferric iron, one of iron's two common chemical forms, to treat iron deficiency.
Supply iron by injection or drip, bypassing the gut, to treat iron deficiency and the anemia it causes.
Anemia medicines that are not iron or vitamin preparations, treating anemia in other ways.
Anemia medicines that are not iron or vitamin preparations, treating anemia in other ways.
Replace blood or body fluids, supply salts or nutrition, or serve for dialysis or rinsing, using blood products or solutions.
Replace blood volume or parts of the blood with products made from human blood, or with substitutes for them.
Blood-derived products other than plasma proteins and blood substitutes, used to replace blood or parts of it.
Dripped into a vein to supply fluid, salts or nutrition, or to rebalance the body's fluids.
Provide nutrition through a vein for people who cannot eat or absorb enough food through the gut.
Medicines for the blood that fit none of the named groups for clotting, bleeding, anemia or blood and fluid replacement.
Medicines for the blood that fit none of the named groups for clotting, bleeding, anemia or blood and fluid replacement.
Prevent or stop sudden swelling attacks of the skin, gut or throat in a rare inherited condition.
Medicines for the blood that fit none of the named groups, treating blood disorders in other ways.
Medicines for the heart and blood vessels: high blood pressure, heart failure, irregular heartbeat, chest pain and high cholesterol.
Medicines for the heart, for example steadying its rhythm, easing chest pain, treating heart failure or raising low blood pressure.
Restore or keep a normal heart rhythm by changing the heart's electrical signals.
Block sodium channels (electrical gates in cells), calming overexcited heart cells to treat abnormal heart rhythms.
Lengthen the heart's electrical recovery between beats, helping restore or keep a normal rhythm in heart rhythm disorders.
Heart rhythm medicines fitting none of the named class I and III subgroups, helping restore or keep a normal rhythm.
Strengthen the heartbeat or tighten blood vessels, supporting the circulation, for example in shock or severe heart failure.
Stimulate the heart and vessels through adrenaline or dopamine receptors, raising low blood pressure or supporting a failing circulation.
Heart stimulants that fit none of the named groups, strengthening the heartbeat or tightening vessels to support the circulation.
Widen blood vessels to ease the heart's workload, for example relieving chest pain (angina) or treating heart failure.
Vessel-widening heart medicines that fit none of the named groups, easing the heart's workload in heart disease.
Heart medicines that fit none of the named cardiac therapy groups, acting on the heart in other ways.
Heart medicines that fit none of the named cardiac groups or subgroups, acting on the heart in other ways.
Lower high blood pressure, including in the lung arteries (pulmonary arterial hypertension).
Act in the brain to damp nerve signals that tighten blood vessels and speed the heart, lowering blood pressure.
Stimulate receptors in the brain that quiet the nerve signals raising blood pressure, lowering it.
Blood pressure-lowering medicines that fit none of the other named groups, including those for high pressure in the lung arteries.
Medicines lowering high blood pressure in other ways, fitting none of the named groups.
Relax narrowed lung arteries or slow their thickening, easing strain on the heart and improving exercise ability.
Make the kidneys remove more water or salt, easing fluid buildup (swelling), heart strain or high blood pressure.
Remove large amounts of water and salt quickly, used for fluid buildup (edema) from heart or kidney disease.
Stop the kidneys reclaiming salt in their tubule loops, flushing out fluid; used for swelling from heart or kidney disease.
Remove fluid while keeping potassium, some by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes the body hold salt and water.
Block aldosterone, a hormone making the body hold salt and water, to treat conditions such as heart failure or swelling.
Medicines that make the kidneys remove more water or salt but fit none of the named diuretic groups.
Block vasopressin, the hormone making the kidneys hold water, so they release more; used, for example, for low blood sodium.
Block adrenaline's effects on the heart, slowing it; mainly for high blood pressure, chest pain, heart failure or rhythm problems.
Single-ingredient medicines blocking adrenaline's effects on the heart; mainly for high blood pressure, chest pain, heart failure or rhythm problems.
Block adrenaline's effects throughout the body, not just the heart; mainly for high blood pressure, chest pain or rhythm problems.
Block a hormone system that tightens blood vessels and holds salt, used for high blood pressure and heart failure.
Single-ingredient blockers of the enzyme making angiotensin II, a vessel-tightening hormone; used for high blood pressure and heart failure.
Single-ingredient blockers of the enzyme making angiotensin II, a vessel-tightening hormone; used for high blood pressure and heart failure.
Single-ingredient medicines that stop angiotensin II, a vessel-tightening hormone, from acting, relaxing vessels to lower high blood pressure.
Single-ingredient medicines that stop angiotensin II, a vessel-tightening hormone, from acting, relaxing vessels to lower high blood pressure.
Contain an angiotensin blocker plus another medicine, such as a water pill, for high blood pressure or heart failure.
Contain an angiotensin blocker and a water pill, for high blood pressure not controlled by one medicine alone.
Relax arteries in two ways, blocking angiotensin II and calcium entry into artery muscle, to lower high blood pressure.
Contain an angiotensin blocker in combinations other than the named pairs, for high blood pressure or heart failure.
Act on the renin-angiotensin hormone system, which tightens vessels and holds salt, in ways other than the named groups.
Block renin, the kidney enzyme that starts the hormone chain tightening blood vessels, to lower high blood pressure.
Medicines acting on the renin-angiotensin hormone system, which tightens vessels and holds salt, that fit none of the named groups.
Lower cholesterol or other blood fats (such as triglycerides) when levels are too high.
Single-ingredient medicines that lower cholesterol or other blood fats (such as triglycerides) when levels are too high.
Bind bile acids in the gut so the liver uses up cholesterol to make more, lowering blood cholesterol.
Lower triglycerides and raise “good” HDL cholesterol with nicotinic acid (niacin, a B vitamin) or related compounds.
Blood-fat medicines that fit none of the named groups, lowering cholesterol or other blood fats in other ways.
Combine a medicine lowering cholesterol or other blood fats with at least one other medicine in one product.
Combine two or more medicines that lower cholesterol or other blood fats, each working differently, in one product.
Medicines for skin problems such as infections, eczema, psoriasis, acne and wounds, mostly applied to the skin itself.
Soften, moisturize or protect the skin, for example against dryness, irritation or harmful sunlight.
Protect the skin from the sun's ultraviolet (UV) rays, which burn skin and cause reactions in people sensitive to light.
Work from inside the body, rather than on the skin, to protect it against the sun's ultraviolet (UV) light.
Help wounds and open sores (ulcers) heal, or clear away dead tissue that slows healing.
Promote healing, helping wounds and open sores close over with new tissue.
Wound-healing medicines that fit none of the other named groups at this level; they help wounds and sores close.
Break down dead tissue in wounds and ulcers with enzymes, cleaning them so they can heal.
Dissolve dead tissue in wounds and ulcers with enzymes that break down proteins, so the wounds can heal.
Used on the skin against bacteria, viruses and other germs; some also treat warts or other abnormal skin growths.
Kill or stop bacteria on the skin, treating bacterial skin infections such as infected cuts.
Skin-applied antibiotics that fit none of the other named groups at this level; they treat bacterial skin infections.
Germ-fighting chemicals other than antibiotics, applied to the skin; some also treat warts or abnormal skin growths.
Applied to the skin against viral infections such as cold sores and warts.
Skin-applied treatments against germs or abnormal skin growths that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Treat acne, the spots and pimples caused by blocked, inflamed hair follicles and oil glands.
Applied to the skin to treat acne, e.g. by unclogging pores, killing acne bacteria or calming inflammation.
Skin-applied acne treatments that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Medicines for skin conditions that fit none of the other skin medicine groups.
Medicines for skin conditions that fit none of the other skin medicine groups.
Treat dermatitis (eczema: itchy, inflamed skin) without steroids, for example by calming an overactive immune system.
Medicines for skin conditions that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Sex hormones and medicines for genital and urinary organs, e.g. vaginal infections, contraception, fertility, menopause, prostate and bladder problems.
Gynecological medicines (for women's reproductive organs) that fit neither the anti-infective nor the sex hormone groups.
Medicines for women's reproductive health outside the anti-infective, sex hormone, womb-contracting and locally applied contraceptive groups.
Medicines for women's reproductive health that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Contraceptives, fertility hormones, menopause treatments and other medicines that act like or against female or male sex hormones.
Hormones that prevent pregnancy by acting throughout the body, for regular use or as emergency contraception after unprotected sex.
Contraceptives combining two types of female hormone, a progestogen and an estrogen, which together stop the monthly egg release.
Taken after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure to help prevent pregnancy, mainly by delaying the release of an egg.
Male sex hormones (androgens) and lab-made look-alikes, used mainly when the body makes too little of its own.
Male sex hormones with a shared steroid structure (3-oxoandrostene), mainly replacing male hormone when the body makes too little.
Female sex hormones (estrogens), mainly to relieve menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, alone or combined with another medicine.
The female sex hormone estrogen on its own, in its natural form or close to it; mainly for menopause symptoms.
A female hormone (estrogen) combined with another medicine in one product, mainly to relieve menopause symptoms.
Stimulate the ovaries or testes to make eggs or sperm; used mainly in fertility treatment.
Hormones that drive egg and sperm production in the ovaries and testes; used mainly in fertility treatment.
Medicines that mimic, block or adjust sex hormone effects but fit none of the main sex hormone groups.
Block or partly mimic the hormone progesterone at its receptors, changing how it controls the womb and pregnancy.
Act like the hormone estrogen in some tissues and block it in others; used mainly for problems after menopause.
Medicines that mimic, block or adjust sex hormone effects but fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Medicines for urinary and male sexual problems, such as overactive bladder, enlarged prostate and erection difficulties.
Medicines for urinary and male sexual problems other than an enlarged prostate, e.g. bladder leaks, urinary stones or erection difficulties.
Reduce urgent, frequent urination and urine leaks, for example by relaxing an overactive bladder muscle.
Help men get or keep an erection, for example by boosting blood flow to the penis.
Medicines for urinary or sexual problems that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Ease urination problems caused by a noncancerous enlarged prostate, common in older men.
Relax muscle in the prostate and bladder outlet by blocking adrenaline-type signals, easing urine flow in an enlarged prostate.
Hormones and hormone blockers besides sex hormones and insulin, e.g. against inflammation or for growth, thyroid, adrenal or calcium disorders.
Mimic or block hormones of the pituitary and hypothalamus, the brain's hormone centers steering growth, fertility and other glands.
Copy or block front-pituitary hormones, which control growth and other glands such as the thyroid and adrenals.
The pituitary's thyroid-stimulating hormone, which prompts thyroid cells to take up iodine; used in thyroid tests and thyroid cancer care.
Supply growth hormone (somatropin) or a look-alike, for poor growth in children or growth hormone deficiency in adults.
Medicines copying or blocking front-pituitary hormones that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Copy or block hormones from the hypothalamus, the brain's hormone control center, which tells the pituitary gland what to release.
Mimic somatostatin, a natural hormone curbing release of growth hormone and other hormones; used e.g. in acromegaly (excess growth hormone).
Block gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain signal that sets off sex hormone production, so sex hormone levels fall quickly.
Adrenal-type steroid hormones acting throughout the body, which calm inflammation or replace missing adrenal hormones, plus cortisol-lowering medicines.
Adrenal-type steroid hormones given on their own, acting throughout the body to calm inflammation or replace missing adrenal hormones.
Act like the body's cortisol, calming inflammation and immune reactions, or replacing it when the adrenal glands fail.
Reduce hormone production by the adrenal glands; used for Cushing's syndrome, where the body makes too much cortisol.
Lower the body's cortisol, e.g. by blocking adrenal enzymes that make it; used for Cushing's syndrome (too much cortisol).
Treat an underactive or overactive thyroid gland, by replacing thyroid hormone or curbing the gland's hormone production.
Replace or mimic thyroid hormone, mainly when the thyroid gland makes too little (underactive thyroid).
Replace or mimic thyroid hormone, mainly when the thyroid gland makes too little (underactive thyroid).
Hormones of the pancreas other than insulin (classed with diabetes medicines), for example ones raising dangerously low blood sugar.
Make the liver release its stored sugar (glycogen) into the blood; used mainly for severe low blood sugar in diabetes.
Make the liver release its stored sugar (glycogen) into the blood; used mainly for severe low blood sugar in diabetes.
Copy or counter the hormones controlling blood calcium and bone renewal; used for osteoporosis, parathyroid disorders and high blood calcium.
Copies of the calcium-setting hormone; they build bone in osteoporosis or replace the hormone when parathyroid glands underperform.
Stimulate new bone in osteoporosis, or restore blood calcium when the parathyroid glands make too little of their hormone.
Lower parathyroid hormone or blood calcium; used for overactive parathyroid glands, e.g. in people on dialysis, and high calcium.
The hormone calcitonin, which slows bone breakdown and lowers blood calcium; used for Paget's disease of bone and high calcium.
Medicines lowering parathyroid hormone or blood calcium that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Medicines that fight or prevent infections, mainly working throughout the body: antibiotics, antifungals, tuberculosis drugs, antivirals, antibodies and vaccines.
Kill or stop bacteria throughout the body; used for bacterial infections such as pneumonia and skin, urinary or bloodstream infections.
A family of broad-acting antibiotics that stop bacteria making proteins; used for many kinds of bacterial infection.
A family of broad-acting antibiotics that stop bacteria making proteins; used for many kinds of bacterial infection.
Cell-wall-breaking (beta-lactam) antibiotics other than penicillins, such as cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams, used against many kinds of bacterial infection.
Cell-wall-breaking antibiotics of the cephalosporin family's third generation, reaching more gut-type bacteria than earlier generations.
Cell-wall-breaking antibiotics of the cephalosporin family's fourth generation, acting against a very broad range of bacteria.
Cell-wall-breaking antibiotics with a single-ring structure that act only on Gram-negative bacteria, a type including many gut and hospital germs.
Very broad-acting cell-wall-breaking antibiotics for serious infections such as pneumonia and urinary or abdominal infections.
Cell-wall-breaking antibiotics: cephalosporins fitting none of the four numbered generations, and penems, a related family.
Three related antibiotic families that stop bacteria making proteins; used e.g. for chest, throat and skin infections.
Antibiotics built on a large ring structure that stop bacteria making proteins; used e.g. for chest, sinus and throat infections.
Potent antibiotics that disrupt how bacteria make proteins; used mainly for serious infections.
Aminoglycoside antibiotics (which disrupt bacterial protein making) that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Antibiotics that block bacteria copying their DNA; used for many infections, e.g. of the urinary tract, chest or skin.
Quinolone antibiotics with added fluorine for broader reach, blocking bacteria copying their DNA; used for many infections.
Antibiotics for use throughout the body that fit none of the main antibiotic families.
Antibiotics that block cell-wall building in bacteria such as staph and strep, including resistant staph (MRSA); used for serious infections.
Antibiotics that break the outer membrane of certain bacteria (Gram-negative); often kept for serious, resistant infections.
Antibiotics for use throughout the body that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Fight fungal infections from inside the body rather than on the skin, e.g. candida (yeast) or aspergillus (mold) infections.
Kill or stop fungi throughout the body; used to treat or prevent yeast and mold infections, including serious ones.
Block fungi from building their cell membranes; used to treat or prevent yeast and mold infections, some life-threatening.
Antifungals for use throughout the body that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Medicines against mycobacteria, slow-growing bacteria behind tuberculosis, leprosy and related infections.
Kill or stop the bacteria that cause tuberculosis (TB), a serious infection mainly of the lungs.
Tuberculosis medicines based on aminosalicylic acid (PAS), which slows the growth of tuberculosis bacteria.
Tuberculosis medicines that fit none of the other named groups at this level; they kill or stop tuberculosis bacteria.
Block viruses from multiplying in the body; used e.g. for HIV, hepatitis B and C, herpes viruses and flu.
Act directly on viruses, blocking steps they need to multiply, e.g. in HIV, hepatitis, herpes or flu.
Fake genetic building blocks that jam how viruses copy their genes; used e.g. for herpes-family infections.
Block an enzyme (protease) viruses need to cut their proteins into working parts; used e.g. for HIV.
Fake building blocks that stop the virus copying its genes into DNA; used for HIV and hepatitis B.
Bind and jam the enzyme HIV uses to copy its genes into DNA; used to treat HIV.
Stop new flu viruses leaving infected cells, limiting spread; used to treat or prevent flu.
Stop HIV from inserting its genes into the infected cell's own DNA, a step the virus needs to multiply.
Block steps the hepatitis C virus needs to multiply; used, often in combinations, to treat hepatitis C infection.
Two or more HIV medicines combined in one product, used against HIV infection.
Antivirals that fit none of the other named groups at this level; they stop viruses entering cells or multiplying.
Ready-made antibodies from human or animal blood, or lab-made, that prevent or fight infections and toxins, or treat immune problems.
Antibodies, pooled from donors or lab-made, for immune deficiency, immune disorders or against specific germs or toxins.
Antibodies pooled from blood donors, replacing missing antibodies in immune deficiency or calming some disorders of the immune system.
Donor antibodies selected for high levels against one target, such as a germ, a toxin or a blood group.
Lab-made antibodies that target bacteria or the toxins they release, to prevent or treat bacterial infections.
Lab-made antibodies that latch onto a virus to help prevent or treat its infection.
Prepare the immune system to recognize and fight a germ, preventing the disease or making it milder.
Train the immune system to recognize disease-causing bacteria or their toxins, preventing the diseases they cause.
Protect against cholera, a severe diarrheal disease spread through contaminated water and food.
Protect against meningococcal bacteria, which cause meningitis and blood poisoning; each vaccine covers one or more of the bacteria's groups.
Protect against whooping cough (pertussis), a severe coughing illness especially dangerous for babies.
Protect against pneumococcal bacteria, a main cause of pneumonia, meningitis and ear infections; each covers a set of strain types.
Train the immune system to recognize disease-causing viruses, preventing the diseases they cause or making them milder.
Protect against viruses that inflame the brain (encephalitis), such as those spread by mosquitoes or ticks.
Protect against flu; seasonal vaccines are updated yearly for new strains, others target pandemic or bird flu.
Protect against viral liver infections (hepatitis), such as hepatitis A and B.
Protect against measles, a highly contagious viral illness, alone or combined with vaccines against other viral diseases.
Protect against rabies, a deadly brain infection spread by animal bites.
Protect babies against rotavirus, a common cause of severe diarrhea in young children.
Protect against the chickenpox virus: against chickenpox itself, or shingles, a painful rash when the dormant virus reawakens.
Protect against human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, to prevent cervical and other cancers and precancers it can cause.
Protect against COVID-19, the illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus.
Protect against chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus causing fever and long-lasting joint pain.
Vaccines that fit none of the other named viral vaccine groups; they train the immune system against a virus.
Vaccines combining protection against bacterial and viral diseases in one product, covering several diseases at once.
Vaccines combining protection against bacterial and viral diseases in one product, covering several diseases at once.
Cancer medicines (chemotherapy, targeted and hormone therapy) and medicines that calm or boost immunity, e.g. for arthritis or transplants.
Medicines that kill cancer cells or stop them growing: chemotherapy, targeted drugs, antibodies, and cell and gene therapies.
Chemotherapy that attaches small chemical (alkyl) groups to DNA, damaging it so that dividing cancer cells die.
DNA-damaging chemotherapy chemically related to mustard gas; it stops cancer cells from dividing.
DNA-damaging chemotherapy of the alkyl sulfonate chemical type, which kills dividing cells such as cancer cells.
DNA-damaging chemotherapy built on a reactive three-atom ring (ethylene imine), which kills dividing cells such as cancer cells.
DNA-damaging chemotherapy of the nitrosourea chemical type, which kills dividing cells such as cancer cells.
DNA-damaging (alkylating) chemotherapy that fits none of the named chemical groups; it kills dividing cells such as cancer cells.
Chemotherapy that mimics the building blocks or vitamins cells need to make DNA, so cancer cells cannot divide.
Look-alikes of folic acid, a vitamin cells need to copy DNA, that block its use so cancer cells cannot divide.
Look-alikes of purines, building blocks of DNA, that stop cancer cells from copying their DNA and dividing.
Look-alikes of pyrimidines, building blocks of DNA and RNA, that stop cancer cells from copying their DNA and dividing.
Chemotherapy made from, or modeled on, substances found in plants and other living things; it stops cancer cells from dividing.
Chemotherapy from the periwinkle (vinca) plant or modeled on it; it blocks the fibers (microtubules) cells need to divide.
Chemotherapy of a chemical type first found in yew trees; it freezes the fibers (microtubules) cells need to divide.
Chemotherapy that blocks topoisomerase 1, an enzyme cells need to untwist DNA when copying it, so cancer cells die.
Cancer chemotherapy derived from plants or other natural sources that fits none of the named natural-product groups.
Substances first found in microbes, like antibiotics, or related to them, used to kill cancer cells rather than germs.
Cancer drugs first found in soil bacteria, or made to resemble them, that slip into DNA and block its copying.
Targeted cancer drugs that block kinases, enzymes that switch on the growth signals cancer cells depend on.
Block the abnormal BCR-ABL enzyme made by a gene fusion in chronic myeloid leukemia and some acute lymphoblastic leukemias.
Block EGFR, a growth-signal receptor overactive in some tumors, by disabling its enzyme inside the cell.
Block BRAF, a growth-signal enzyme that becomes overactive after certain gene changes in some tumors.
Block ALK, a growth-signal enzyme that some tumors switch on through a rearrangement of its gene.
Block MEK, a relay enzyme in a signal chain that drives cell growth and is overactive in some tumors.
Block cyclin-dependent kinases, enzymes that push cells through the steps of division, so cancer cells stop multiplying.
Block mTOR, an enzyme acting as a master switch for cell growth and division, to slow tumor growth.
Block HER2, a growth-signal receptor that some tumors make too much of, by disabling its enzyme inside the cell.
Block JAK enzymes, which relay growth and immune signals inside cells and are overactive in some bone marrow cancers.
Block receptors for VEGF, the signal tumors use to grow the new blood vessels that feed them.
Block BTK, an enzyme that B cells (a type of white blood cell), including cancerous ones, need to multiply.
Block PI3K, an enzyme that relays growth and survival signals and is overactive in some tumors.
Block FGFR, growth-signal receptors that gene changes can abnormally switch on in some tumors.
Block MET, a growth-signal receptor that gene changes can abnormally switch on in some tumors.
Kinase blockers for cancer that fit none of the named target groups; kinases are enzymes switching on growth signals.
Cancer treatments using lab-made antibodies that flag tumor cells, block growth signals or unleash immunity; some deliver chemotherapy to tumors.
Antibodies that destroy B cells, a type of white blood cell, including cancerous ones, by attaching to their CD20 protein.
Antibodies that attach to CD22, a protein on B cells (a type of white blood cell), to kill cancerous ones.
Antibodies that attach to CD38, a protein abundant on some blood cancer cells, to help destroy those cells.
Antibodies that attach to HER2, a growth-signal receptor some tumors make too much of, to slow or kill those tumors.
Antibodies that attach to EGFR, a growth-signal receptor on many cancer cells, to block its signals or kill those cells.
Antibodies that release an immune brake (PD-1 or its partner PD-L1) so the immune system attacks cancer cells.
Antibodies that block VEGF, the signal tumors use to grow new blood vessels, or its receptor (VEGFR).
Cancer antibodies, alone or carrying a cell-killing drug, that fit none of the named antibody groups.
Two or more cancer antibodies (with or without an attached cell-killing drug) combined in one medicine.
Cancer medicines that fit none of the chemotherapy, kinase inhibitor or antibody groups, sorted into smaller subgroups.
Drugs that make diseased tissue sensitive to light or radiation, so a light or radiation treatment can destroy it.
Vitamin A-related drugs (retinoids) used against cancer; they push cancer cells to mature or die.
Block the proteasome, the cell's protein-recycling machine, so unneeded proteins pile up and kill cancer cells.
Block histone deacetylases, enzymes that keep genes switched off, reawakening genes that restrain cancer cell growth.
Block the hedgehog pathway, a growth signal active in embryos that some tumors switch back on.
Block PARP, a DNA-repair enzyme, killing cancer cells that already repair DNA poorly, e.g. through BRCA gene changes.
Cancer treatments made of living cells or genes, e.g. a patient's own immune cells modified to attack the cancer.
Block a faulty IDH enzyme, altered by gene changes in some tumors, that makes a cancer-promoting substance.
Cancer medicines that fit none of the named cancer groups or subgroups, whatever their chemistry or way of working.
Two or more cancer medicines of any kind combined in one product.
Cancer treatments that add, lower or block hormones, as some tumors, often of the breast or prostate, depend on them.
Slow hormone-driven cancers with hormones or look-alikes, e.g. ones that shut down the body's own sex hormone production.
Mimic a brain hormone (GnRH) so constantly that the body stops making sex hormones such as testosterone and estrogen.
Block hormones or their production to slow hormone-driven cancers, e.g. estrogen in breast cancer or testosterone in prostate cancer.
Stop estrogen from acting on its receptor in tumor cells, slowing hormone-sensitive cancers such as many breast cancers.
Stop male hormones (androgens) such as testosterone from acting on cancer cells, e.g. in prostate cancer.
Hormone-blocking cancer treatments that fit none of the named groups: estrogen blockers, male-hormone blockers and estrogen-production blockers.
Medicines that boost the immune system or blood cell production: growth factors, interferons, interleukins and others.
Medicines that boost the immune system or blood cell production: growth factors, interferons, interleukins and others.
Growth factors that make the bone marrow produce more white blood cells, e.g. when chemotherapy has lowered them.
Medicines based on interferons, the body's signaling proteins that fight viruses and adjust immune responses.
Medicines based on interleukins, the body's signaling proteins, used to stimulate immune cells or blood cell production.
Immune-stimulating medicines that fit none of the named groups (white-cell growth factors, interferons, interleukins).
Calm the immune system in autoimmune diseases, e.g. arthritis, psoriasis, bowel inflammation, multiple sclerosis, and to prevent transplant rejection.
Calm the immune system in autoimmune diseases, e.g. arthritis, psoriasis, bowel inflammation, multiple sclerosis, and to prevent transplant rejection.
Immune-calming medicines that act on specific parts of the immune system rather than suppressing it broadly.
Block TNF-alpha, an immune signaling protein that drives inflammation in autoimmune diseases, e.g. of the joints, skin or gut.
Block interleukins, immune messenger proteins that drive inflammation, or their receptors, calming overactive immune responses.
Stop T cells, key immune cells, from switching on by blocking calcineurin, an enzyme they need.
Act on receptors for S1P, a fat-based signal, keeping certain immune cells in lymph nodes so fewer reach inflamed tissues.
Block JAK enzymes, which relay the signals of many inflammation-driving messengers inside immune cells.
Lab-made antibodies that calm the immune system by attaching to specific targets, e.g. proteins on immune cells.
Block mTOR, an enzyme acting as a growth switch that immune cells need to multiply, calming the immune system.
Block complement, a chain of immune proteins that can wrongly attack the body's own cells and tissues.
Block DHODH, an enzyme fast-multiplying immune cells need to make DNA building blocks, slowing their multiplication.
Block FcRn, the receptor that recycles antibodies, so the body clears them faster, including harmful self-attacking ones.
Immune-calming medicines that fit none of the named immunosuppressant groups, whatever their chemistry or way of working.
Medicines for bones, joints and muscles, e.g. against inflammation and pain, muscle spasm, gout or bone diseases.
Medicines that ease inflammation and pain in joints and muscles, e.g. in arthritis and other rheumatic diseases.
Ease inflammation and pain in joints and muscles without steroids, e.g. NSAIDs, which block COX enzymes making inflammation signals.
Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) that mainly block COX-2, an enzyme making inflammation signals, and less so the stomach-protecting COX-1.
Medicines that relax muscles, by acting on nerve-muscle signals, on the brain and spinal cord, or on muscle directly.
Relax muscles by blocking, at the junction between nerve and muscle, the signal that makes muscles contract.
Muscle relaxants that act where nerves meet muscles but fit none of the named chemical groups.
Relax muscles by acting inside the muscle cells themselves rather than on nerves.
Relax muscles by stopping calcium release inside muscle cells, as dantrolene does.
Medicines for gout that lower uric acid, whose crystals inflame joints, or calm the inflammation the crystals cause.
Medicines for gout that lower uric acid, whose crystals inflame joints, or calm the inflammation the crystals cause.
Lower uric acid by cutting its production, e.g. by blocking xanthine oxidase, the enzyme making it; used mainly for gout.
Lower uric acid by helping the kidneys pass more of it into urine; used for gout.
Calm the joint inflammation caused by uric acid crystals in gout, without changing uric acid levels.
Gout medicines that fit none of the named groups (cutting uric acid production, passing more into urine, calming inflammation).
Medicines for bone diseases such as osteoporosis, e.g. by changing how the body builds and breaks down bone.
Change how bone is built, broken down or mineralized (hardened with calcium), e.g. to strengthen bones in osteoporosis.
Bind to bone and slow the cells that break it down, reducing bone loss, e.g. in osteoporosis.
Products combining a bisphosphonate, which slows bone loss, with one or more other substances.
Versions of the body's signaling proteins that trigger new bone formation, used to help bone grow or heal.
Medicines that change bone building, breakdown or hardening but fit none of the named groups (bisphosphonates, bone growth proteins).
Medicines for muscle, bone or joint disorders that fit none of the main named musculoskeletal groups.
Medicines for muscle, bone or joint disorders that fit none of the main named musculoskeletal groups.
Medicines made of enzymes, proteins that break down specific substances, used for muscle, bone or joint disorders.
Medicines for muscle, bone or joint disorders that fit none of the named musculoskeletal groups or subgroups.
Medicines acting on the brain and nerves: anesthetics, painkillers, and medicines for epilepsy, Parkinson's, mental illness, dementia and addiction.
Medicines that numb one area (local anesthetics) or are used to put patients fully under for surgery (general anesthesia).
Medicines used in general anesthesia, putting patients fully under or blocking pain during surgery.
Strong opioids, which act on the body's opioid receptors, used during anesthesia to block pain.
Numb one area of the body by stopping its nerves from sending pain and other signals.
Numbing medicines (local anesthetics) of the amide chemical type, which block nerve signals in the area treated.
Numbing medicines (local anesthetics) that fit none of the named chemical groups (esters and amides).
Medicines for pain: opioids, other painkillers and fever reducers, and medicines to prevent or stop migraine attacks.
Painkillers that act on the body's opioid receptors, the targets of its own pain-relieving chemicals.
Opioid painkillers built on a shared chemical core (phenylpiperidine), acting on the body's opioid receptors.
Painkillers and fever reducers that are neither opioids nor migraine medicines.
Painkillers and fever reducers chemically related to salicylic acid, a substance first made from willow bark.
Calm overactive nerves by reducing the release of their chemical messengers, which eases nerve pain.
Non-opioid painkillers and fever reducers that fit none of the named groups.
Medicines that stop migraine attacks or prevent them from happening as often.
Stop migraine attacks by activating serotonin (5HT1) receptors on nerves or blood vessels involved in migraine.
Block CGRP, a nerve messenger behind migraine pain, or its receptor, to stop migraine attacks or prevent them.
Medicines that prevent or reduce seizures in epilepsy by calming overactive electrical signaling in the brain.
Medicines that prevent or reduce seizures in epilepsy by calming overactive electrical signaling in the brain.
Antiseizure medicines of the carboxamide chemical type, which calm overexcited nerve cells in the brain.
Antiseizure medicines chemically related to fatty acids, which calm overexcited nerve cells in the brain.
Antiseizure medicines for epilepsy that fit none of the named chemical groups, whatever their way of working.
Medicines that ease Parkinson's disease symptoms by boosting dopamine, the brain messenger it depletes, or in other ways.
Boost dopamine signaling in the brain by replacing, releasing or mimicking dopamine, or slowing its breakdown, e.g. in Parkinson's.
Replace missing dopamine with dopa (levodopa) or its derivatives, which the brain converts into dopamine.
Mimic dopamine by activating its receptors in the brain, making up for the dopamine lost in Parkinson's disease.
Block an enzyme (MAO-B) that breaks down dopamine, so more stays active in the brain; used for Parkinson's.
Dopamine-boosting medicines for Parkinson's disease that fit none of the named dopamine-acting groups.
Parkinson's medicines that fit none of the named groups (acetylcholine blockers, dopamine-boosting medicines).
Parkinson's medicines that fit none of the named groups (acetylcholine blockers, dopamine-boosting medicines).
Medicines that calm the brain: antipsychotics for psychosis, anti-anxiety medicines, and sleep medicines and sedatives.
Reduce psychosis symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, typically by damping dopamine signals, e.g. in schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.
Antipsychotics of the indole chemical type; like other antipsychotics, they ease psychosis symptoms such as hallucinations.
Antipsychotics sharing a similar multi-ring chemical core; like other antipsychotics, they ease psychosis symptoms such as hallucinations.
Medicines for psychosis (antipsychotics) that fit none of the named groups; they ease symptoms such as hallucinations.
Medicines that help people fall or stay asleep (hypnotics) or calm and relax them (sedatives).
Sleep medicines and sedatives of the benzodiazepine type, which strengthen the effect of GABA, the brain's calming messenger.
Sleep medicines that are not benzodiazepines chemically but, like them, strengthen the effect of GABA, the brain's calming messenger.
Activate receptors for melatonin, the body's own sleep-timing hormone, to help regulate sleep.
Block the receptors for orexin, a brain signal that keeps people awake, helping them fall and stay asleep.
Sleep medicines and sedatives that fit none of the named groups, whatever their chemistry or way of working.
Medicines acting on mood, alertness or memory: antidepressants, stimulants and ADHD medicines, and dementia medicines.
Medicines for depression that adjust brain messengers such as serotonin; some also treat anxiety.
Medicines for depression that fit none of the named antidepressant groups, whatever their chemistry or way of working.
Stimulants and related medicines that raise alertness or attention, e.g. for ADHD, and nootropics meant to improve thinking.
Boost the brain's alerting messengers, such as norepinephrine and dopamine, increasing alertness and attention, e.g. in ADHD.
Stimulants chemically related to xanthine, a natural compound; they typically block adenosine, a brain messenger that promotes drowsiness.
Stimulants, ADHD medicines or nootropics (meant to improve thinking) that fit none of the named groups.
Medicines for dementia, e.g. in Alzheimer's disease, that ease its symptoms or slow its course.
Raise acetylcholine, a brain messenger important for memory, by slowing its breakdown, easing dementia symptoms.
Dementia medicines that do not fit the named group of acetylcholine-breakdown blockers, whatever their way of working.
Nervous system medicines that fit none of the main groups, including those for addiction or dizziness (vertigo).
Help people overcome addiction, for example to smoking, alcohol or opioids, often by easing cravings or withdrawal.
Help people stop smoking or other nicotine use, e.g. by easing cravings and withdrawal symptoms.
Help people stop or cut down drinking alcohol, e.g. by reducing cravings or making drinking less rewarding or unpleasant.
Treat opioid addiction, e.g. as substitutes that act on opioid receptors to ease withdrawal and cravings.
Nervous system medicines that fit none of the named groups or subgroups, whatever their way of working.
Nervous system medicines that fit none of the named groups or subgroups, whatever their way of working.
Medicines against parasites: malaria parasites and other single-celled ones, worms, and lice or scabies mites, plus insect repellents.
Kill single-celled parasites (protozoa); used for infections such as malaria, amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness.
Kill the single-celled parasites that cause malaria, a disease spread by mosquito bites; used to treat or prevent it.
Fast-acting malaria medicines based on artemisinin, a sweet wormwood plant substance, in products with no other active ingredient.
Pair artemisinin (from sweet wormwood) or a derivative with a longer-acting partner drug; used for malaria that is not severe.
Kill or expel parasitic worms, such as roundworms, tapeworms and flukes, that live in the gut or other tissues.
Act against roundworms (nematodes), such as pinworms, hookworms and whipworms, that infect the gut or other tissues.
Roundworm medicines with a shared chemical structure (imidazothiazole) that paralyze the worms so the body can expel them.
Medicines for the nose, throat, airways and lungs: inhalers for asthma and COPD (chronic lung disease), cough and allergy remedies.
Medicines for the nose, applied inside it or acting through the body, e.g. against a blocked, runny or itchy nose.
Medicines applied inside the nose, for example to ease congestion, allergy or inflammation, as in colds or hay fever.
Calm inflammation inside the nose with cortisol-like steroids, as in hay fever and other nasal allergies.
Shrink swollen nasal blood vessels by acting through the whole body, unblocking the nose, as in colds or hay fever.
Act like adrenaline throughout the body, narrowing swollen blood vessels in the nose to unblock it.
Open narrowed airways or calm their inflammation; used for asthma and COPD (chronic lung disease).
Inhaled, adrenaline-like medicines that relax airway muscles to open the airways; used for asthma and COPD.
Inhaled airway openers acting on the lungs' adrenaline receptors (beta-2) more than the heart's; used for asthma and COPD.
Inhalers pairing an adrenaline-like airway opener with an anti-inflammatory steroid or certain other drugs; used for asthma and COPD.
Inhalers joining two airway openers that work in different ways, sometimes plus a steroid; used for COPD and asthma.
Inhaled medicines for asthma and COPD that are not adrenaline-like, such as steroids and nerve-signal blockers that open airways.
Inhaled airway openers that block acetylcholine, a nerve signal that tightens airway muscles; used for COPD and asthma.
A catch-all for inhaled asthma and COPD medicines that fit none of the other inhaled groups.
Asthma and COPD medicines taken by mouth or injected rather than inhaled, outside the separate group of adrenaline-like ones.
A catch-all for asthma and COPD medicines given by mouth or injection that fit none of the other groups.
Ease coughing, loosen mucus so it is easier to cough up, or relieve other cold symptoms.
Help bring up mucus from the airways, for example by thinning it; not combined with a cough suppressant.
Thin or loosen sticky mucus in the airways so it is easier to cough up.
Reduce the urge to cough, as in a dry, irritating cough; not combined with a medicine that loosens mucus.
A catch-all for medicines that reduce the urge to cough but fall outside the opium-related group.
Block histamine, a chemical behind allergy symptoms, throughout the body; used for allergies such as hay fever and hives.
Block histamine, a chemical behind allergy symptoms, throughout the body; used for allergies such as hay fever and hives.
A catch-all for allergy medicines that block histamine throughout the body but fit none of the main chemical families.
Airway and lung medicines outside the main groups, such as breathing stimulants and lung surfactants that help newborns' lungs open.
Airway and lung medicines outside the main groups, such as breathing stimulants and lung surfactants that help newborns' lungs open.
A catch-all for airway and lung medicines that fit none of the other respiratory groups.
Medicines for the eyes and ears, such as drops against infection, inflammation, allergy or glaucoma.
Medicines used in or on the eye, e.g. for glaucoma, macular degeneration, allergy, inflammation, infection, eye exams or surgery.
Fight eye infections caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi or other germs.
Stop viruses multiplying in the eye; used for virus infections of the eye's surface or retina, such as herpes.
A catch-all for eye medicines against infection that fit none of the other infection groups.
Calm inflammation of the eye, for example after eye surgery or inside the eye (uveitis).
Cortisol-like steroids that calm eye inflammation, in eye products with no other active ingredient.
Eye medicines that calm inflammation but are not steroids, for example from the common painkiller family (NSAIDs).
Lower the pressure inside the eye to protect the optic nerve, as in glaucoma, or narrow the pupil (miotics).
Block an enzyme the eye needs to make fluid, lowering eye pressure; used for glaucoma and raised eye pressure.
Block adrenaline's effect in the eye to reduce fluid production, lowering eye pressure; used for glaucoma and raised eye pressure.
Mimic a natural body substance to help fluid drain from the eye; used for glaucoma and raised eye pressure.
A catch-all for glaucoma medicines that lower eye pressure but fit none of the main groups.
Widen the pupil or relax the eye's focusing muscle, for example for eye examinations or eye surgery.
Block a nerve signal (acetylcholine) in the eye, widening the pupil and relaxing the eye's focusing muscle.
Adrenaline-like eye medicines that widen the pupil, for example for eye examinations or surgery; not those for glaucoma.
Ease red, itchy or watery eyes from allergy or irritation, by shrinking swollen blood vessels or blocking allergic reactions.
A catch-all for eye allergy medicines that are not adrenaline-like decongestants; used for itchy, red, watery allergic eyes.
Treat diseased blood vessels at the back of the eye that threaten sight, as in wet age-related macular degeneration.
Curb the growth of new, leaky blood vessels in the eye, as in wet age-related macular degeneration.
A catch-all for eye medicines that fit none of the other eye groups.
A catch-all for eye medicines that fit none of the other eye groups.
Medicines that fit no single body system: antidotes, allergen treatments, diagnostic and imaging agents, and radioactive medicines.
Controlled amounts of what a person is allergic to, given to build tolerance (allergen immunotherapy).
Controlled amounts of what a person is allergic to, given to build tolerance (allergen immunotherapy).
Extracts of what a person is allergic to, given in controlled amounts to build tolerance (immunotherapy).
Treatments that fit no other group, such as antidotes, iron removers, and binders removing excess potassium or phosphate.
Treatments that fit no other group, such as antidotes, iron removers, and binders removing excess potassium or phosphate.
Counteract poisons or overdoses, or reverse the effects of a medicine when they need to end quickly.
Bind excess iron so the body can remove it; used for iron overload, often from repeated blood transfusions.
Lower too-high blood potassium or phosphate, a common problem in kidney disease, for example by binding it in the gut.
Protect healthy tissue from harm caused by cancer medicines or radiation therapy, or limit that harm.
A catch-all for treatments that fit no other group anywhere in the drug classification.
Substances given to diagnose rather than treat, for example to test for infections or check how a hormone gland works.
Diagnostic substances other than urine tests, for example to check how glands or organs work, or to detect tuberculosis.
Check how well the pituitary, a hormone gland below the brain, releases its hormones.
Show whether the immune system reacts to tuberculosis bacteria, a sign of infection, for example through a skin test.
A catch-all for diagnostic substances, used to detect disease or check body functions, that fit no specific test group.
Given to make organs, blood vessels and abnormal areas show more clearly on X-ray, CT, MRI or ultrasound scans.
Agents that make tissues and blood vessels stand out more clearly on MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans.
Weakly magnetic (paramagnetic) compounds that brighten tissues on MRI scans, helping show blood vessels and abnormal areas.
Tiny gas-filled bubbles that reflect sound waves strongly, making blood or body cavities stand out on ultrasound scans.
Tiny gas-filled bubbles that reflect sound waves strongly, making blood or body cavities stand out on ultrasound scans.
Tracers with a small radioactive label that scanners detect, showing how organs work or where disease such as cancer sits.
Radioactive tracers for scans of the brain and spinal cord, showing how they work or changes caused by disease.
Brain scan tracers labeled with radioactive iodine (123I), which scanners detect to help diagnose brain and nerve diseases.
A catch-all for brain and spinal cord scan tracers labeled with neither technetium-99m nor iodine-123.
Radioactive tracers that gather at sites of infection or inflammation, showing on scans where it sits in the body.

Radioactive tracers that help scans show where tumors are and whether cancer has spread.
Tumor-detecting tracers labeled with technetium-99m, the most widely used radioactive scan label.
Tumor-detecting tracers labeled with radioactive indium-111, which scanners detect to show where tumors are.

A catch-all for diagnostic radioactive products that fit none of the organ or disease groups.
Radioactive medicines that treat disease by delivering radiation from inside the body, for example to cancers or inflamed joints.
Radioactive agents that collect where cancer has spread to bone, used to ease the pain it causes.
Radioactive agents that collect where cancer has spread to bone, used to ease the pain it causes.
A catch-all for radioactive treatments other than those for inflamed joints or bone pain from cancer.
Radioactive treatments carrying iodine-131, whose radiation kills the diseased cells where the medicine collects.
A catch-all for radioactive treatments that are not iodine-131 compounds and fit none of the other radiation-treatment groups.
